attacks.claim: The takedown purge races with asynchronous derivative generation. A queued, retrying, or backfill `make_responsive_set` task can recreate derivatives of a purged image after `purge_image` finishes, and CloudFront will serve them. There is no tombstone, task cancellation, or pre-write check of takedown state, and the only test covers an already-complete set.
attacks.evidence: "It is extended to delete every key under the image's `<id>-` prefix and invalidate `/media/YYYY/MM/<id>-*`. Test: purge an image with a full responsive set; assert zero remaining keys" (ABSENT: tombstone/exclusion for purged ids, test for purge racing with the task or backfill)

attacks.claim: The success target (p75 mobile LCP ≤ 2.5 s) is contradicted by the plan's own prototype, which reached 2.6 s. The plan gives no evidence the target is reachable and no fallback or revised target.
attacks.evidence: "p75 LCP 3.9 s → 2.6 s" vs. "CrUX p75 mobile LCP on article pages ≤ 2.5 s within 6 weeks of 100%"

attacks.claim: The `<picture>` gate depends on `has_responsive_set`, but the plan does not say the flag is set only after all 11 derivatives are written and verified. If it is set early or a write fails, `<source>` URLs 404, and browsers choose a source by type support, not by load success, so they will not fall back to the JPEG.
attacks.evidence: "`<picture>` is rendered only when `image.has_responsive_set` is true (set by the task)." (ABSENT: flag ordering relative to the final write, post-write verification)

attacks.claim: The backfill has no headroom and no overrun plan. 310,000 × 0.9 s ÷ 8 workers ≈ 9.7 h against two 5 h windows, using a prototype median with no retries, tail latency, or hardware parity. There is no progress metric or plan if it is unfinished after night two. The 'publishing is never delayed' claim also rests on a Celery queue name, not dedicated capacity, on nodes shared with publishing.
attacks.evidence: "≈ 9.7 h, run over two nights (01:00–06:00) on a separate low-priority Celery queue, so publishing tasks are never delayed."

attacks.claim: There are no resource bounds on the new task. No time limit, peak memory figure, or concurrency cap is given for AVIF encodes of up to 40 MP originals, four at a time per node on workers that also run publishing tasks. A hung or oversized encode could starve or OOM those nodes. Failures are also retried and alerted per image with no aggregation or auto-pause, so a systemic fault could fan out across the 310,000-image backfill.
attacks.evidence: "`make_responsive_set` failures (3 retries, then alert to #web-alerts...)" (ABSENT: soft/hard time limits, memory per task, circuit breaker)

attacks.claim: The plan strips all metadata but never says EXIF orientation is applied to the pixels first. Phone portraits and HEIC uploads could render rotated in the new derivatives, and crop/focal coordinates may not match the oriented image.
attacks.evidence: "colour is converted to sRGB, then all metadata is stripped (`strip=True`)" (ABSENT: auto-rotate/orientation handling)

attacks.claim: The wire-photo licensing conclusion is load-bearing, yet it rests only on an internal photo-desk confirmation. The licence terms are not cited, and wire licences commonly restrict derivatives and new copies. Metadata stripping may also remove credit fields the licences require.
attacks.evidence: "Extra sizes and formats of the same licensed image for the same display use are covered by the current licences (photo desk confirmation on WEB-778, Oct 19)."

attacks.claim: Untrusted image bytes, including HEIC via libheif, are parsed in workers with S3 write credentials. `VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED` is not a sandbox, and the plan mentions no least-privilege IAM or isolation. Uploads are limited to authenticated staff, which lowers the risk.
attacks.evidence: "workers run with `VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED=1`" (ABSENT: process isolation, least-privilege IAM)

attacks.claim: The candidate sets are inconsistent. AVIF and WebP go to 1600 px but the JPEG `srcset` stops at 1200 px, so fallback browsers get lower resolution on high-DPI screens. The `<source>` elements are also not specified with their own `srcset` and `sizes`.
attacks.evidence: "JPEG at 480/800/1200 px and AVIF (q 50) and WebP (q 75) at 480/800/1200/1600 px"

attacks.claim: The takedown sequence of S3 delete then CloudFront invalidation has no stated ordering or retry if the invalidation fails. There is also no dry-run or versioning for mistaken purges, and no migration is described for the new `has_responsive_set` field.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: invalidation failure handling, dry-run/confirmation for `purge_image`, migration for `has_responsive_set`

attacks.claim: `width`/`height` come from 'stored dimensions', which is ambiguous. If they are the original's rather than the crop's, the CLS goal fails. Alpha flattening for PNG-to-JPEG is also unspecified.
attacks.evidence: "gains `width`/`height` from stored dimensions to prevent layout shift"

attacks.claim: The image counts do not reconcile. About 9,000 uploads a month over 24 months is about 216,000, not the 310,000 in backfill scope. The cost sections also omit S3 PUT and invalidation charges, and re-crop derivatives are never reclaimed.
attacks.evidence: "~9,000 new uploads" vs. "images used by articles published in the last 24 months (310,000 of 1.27M)"
